1603-1733

Caption This

Founding the English Colonies

1

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

An ad for Virginia from 1609

Not done

What you’re looking at: A hand-colored title page from a pamphlet printed in London in 1609. The big words say “Nova Britannia. Offering most excellent fruites by Planting in Virginia.” Below the words is a large sailing ship with flags on the waves.

Heads up: The first Virginia settlers faced hunger and disease. Aim your joke at the ad and its big promises. Never joke about people who got sick, starved, or died.

  • Read the big words at the top. Who is this page trying to talk to?
  • Look at the ship. Why would an ad for Virginia show a ship?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 2 of 5

John Winthrop, the Puritan leader

Not done

What you’re looking at: A painted portrait of a man with a dark beard and brown hair that reaches his shoulders. He wears a black coat and a wide white lace collar. His face looks serious. Norton’s image description says this is John Winthrop, a Puritan leader.

Heads up: This is a real person. Aim your joke at the big white collar, the serious mood, or the idea of building a perfect town. Never joke about his face or body.

  • Look at his face and his collar. What kind of mood does the artist show?
  • Winthrop wanted a model community that everyone would watch. What kinds of rules might that lead to?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: PuritansMassachusetts Bay Colony
Image 3 of 5

A map of New Amsterdam

Not done

What you’re looking at: A colored map drawn from above. It shows a small Dutch town on the tip of an island. Houses and gardens sit in neat blocks. A canal runs through the middle, a fort stands at the left end, and ships float in the water. A long wall runs along the right side. A label in the corner says “Redraft of the Castello Plan, New Amsterdam in 1660.”

Heads up: Norton says enslaved Africans were bought and sold in this town. Aim your joke at the map, the canal, or the small size of the town. Never joke about enslaved people or any group of people.

  • Find the canal, the fort, and the wall. Why might a town need all three?
  • Look at the ships. How might a town like this make money?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: New Netherland
Image 4 of 5

A painting of a Virginia wedding

Not done

What you’re looking at: A large painting of a crowded room. In the middle, a woman in a red and white dress holds hands with a man in dark clothes. A man in a gray robe raises his hand over them. English settlers and Native people stand and sit all around and watch. Norton’s image description says this is Pocahontas marrying John Rolfe.

Heads up: This is a serious one. The painting shows real people and a real marriage. Write one clear line about the scene. No jokes about Pocahontas, Native peoples, or how anyone looks or dresses.

  • Look at who is in the room. Who looks English? Who looks Powhatan? Where is everyone standing?
  • This is a painting, not a photo. An artist chose what to show. What might the artist want you to feel?

Image 5 of 5

An early view of Savannah, Georgia

Not done

What you’re looking at: A colored drawing of a new town seen from far away. Rows of small houses with red roofs stand in neat lines on flat ground at the top of a bluff. A thick forest surrounds the town. Below the bluff, a wide river has two big sailing ships and small rowboats.

  • Look at how the houses are lined up. Does this look like a town that just grew, or one that someone planned?
  • Look at the forest and the river. Why might a new colony need both?
